query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Minor refractory element (Mo) incorporation to enhance solid-solution strengthening and microstructural stability.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase Ti–Ni based high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition (approximately 2–5 at.%) of molybdenum into the alloy composition during melting, ensuring homogenous distribution as confirmed by thermodynamic modeling (e.g., CALPHAD).
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., 800–1200°C) conducted in inert atmospheres; the overall composition remains predominantly Ti and Ni with the minor Mo addition.
generation.structural_mediator: A stabilized solid-solution matrix in which homogeneously distributed Mo atoms create local lattice distortions that reinforce the matrix and inhibit the coarsening of microstructural features.
generation.mechanism: Mo acts as a strong solid-solution strengthener by increasing the melting point locally and impeding dislocation motion. Its presence retards thermal softening and helps delay the coarsening process of microstructural features, resulting in improved high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Ti–Ni–Mo alloy (with 2–5 at.% Mo) will demonstrate significantly enhanced yield strength and reduced thermal softening under high-temperature conditions compared to the Mo-free Ti–Ni HEA.
generation.baseline: The original Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy without Mo additions, which displays unestablished or suboptimal high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Applicable to Ti–Ni HEAs where the minor Mo addition can be maintained in a single-phase solid solution; effective in temperature regimes (800–1200°C) where dislocation-mediated deformation is dominant.
generation.uncertainty: Although evidence from other HEA systems supports Mo’s strengthening role, the exact quantitative effect in a Ti–Ni system may require precise control to avoid secondary phase precipitation. CALPHAD analysis and microstructural studies are essential to confirm phase stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of samples: one series of the base Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy and one series with a controlled 2–5 at.% Mo addition. Conduct elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., at 900–1100°C) and perform detailed microstructural analyses (XRD, TEM) to assess phase stability.
measurements: Elevated-temperature yield strength and creep rate
Microstructural evolution and detection of any secondary phases
Lattice parameter measurements confirming Mo in solid solution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength and creep resistance compared to the Mo-free baseline, or if deleterious phases form, the hypothesis is rejected.

Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites [].
